chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Sayf ibn Umeyra, from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about a man who sought a garment from another man using a 'bi'ina' (buy-back) arrangement. The seller said, 'I do not have it with me, but here are dirhams; take them and buy with them.' So he took them and bought a garment as he desired, then came back to sell it to him. The Imam (peace be upon him) said: 'Is it not that if the garment deteriorates, it is from the wealth of the one who gave him the dirhams?' I said, 'Yes.' He said: 'If he wishes, he buys it, and if he wishes, he does not buy it.' I said, 'So there is no problem with it.'

key_terms.بِعِينَةٍ: A commercial transaction involving a buy-back or deferred sale arrangement
key_terms.دَرَاهِمُ: Dirhams, silver coins used as currency
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no problem with it; it is permissible

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on bi'ina (buy-back) transactions in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) validates a specific form of *bi'ina* where the buyer advances cash to purchase goods for the seller, clarifying that the risk of loss remains with the buyer and the seller’s subsequent repurchase is optional. This ruling highlights the flexibility in early Shia commercial jurisprudence, distinguishing it from stricter interpretations that might view such structures as usurious (*riba*) if the repurchase were obligatory. The Imam’s affirmation underscores the principle that the transaction’s validity hinges on the actual transfer of ownership and risk, rather than the mere intent to repurchase.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Ali Bin Al Hakam, from Sayf Bin Umeyra, from Mansour Bin Hazim who said,

‘I asked Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> about a man who seeks a cloth from a man, with a buy-back (بِعِينَةٍ). So he says, ‘It is not with me, and these are Dirhams, so take these and buy with these’. So he takes them and buys some cloth just as he wanted, then comes over with it in order for him to buy from it’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Is it not that if the cloth were to go away (deteriorate), so it would be from the wealth of the one who gave him the Dirhams?’ I said, ‘Yes’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘If he so desires to he buys, and if he so desires to, he does not buy, then there is no problem with it’.
en.sarwar: 3. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Sayf ibn ‘Amirah from Mansur ibn Hazim who has said the following: “

This is concerning my question before abu ‘ Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about the case of a man who asks another man for a cloth on the basis of ‘Aynah and he says, ‘I do not have it but take these dirhams and buy the cloth.’ He takes the dirhams and buys a cloth as he wants, then comes to him so that he buys it from him. He (the Imam) said, Ts it the case that if the cloth is lost it is from the assets of the one who gives dirham?’ I replied, ‘Yes, that is the case.’ He (the Imam) asked, ‘If it is possible that if he wants he buys it, if he does not want he does not buy, then it is not unlawful.’”
